title: Why Insurance Needs AI That Fulfills Requests End-To-End
summary: AI agents make insurance requests effortless, but manual handoffs still slow fulfillment. Why policy servicing needs AI that fulfills requests end to end.
body_markdown:
It seems like insurance is heading toward a choke point. The rise of AI has made it almost effortless for customers to ask for things, while the work of fulfilling those requests still moves through manual handoffs, disconnected systems, and layers of approval. We saw this up close recently, when we needed a certificate of insurance (COI) for our own office. Writing the request took a minute, but getting the certificate back took 27 days.


## **Friction used to keep demand in check**


For years, asking your insurance provider for anything took real effort: you had to work out who to contact, explain what you needed in terms they'd recognize, and then follow up if the reply didn't come on time. So, naturally, people rationed their requests.


If a change wasn't urgent, it often waited until renewal. If shopping for a new provider meant a week of calls and forms, most businesses stayed where they were. Nobody designed it this way, but that friction worked as a hidden limit on demand. And because demand stayed low, a lot of slow back-office work never had to get faster.


## **How AI is taking that limit away**


Now an AI agent can draft the email, pull the right policy details, compare options across providers, submit a change request, and chase a response two days later without anyone having to remember to do it.


> *“The small requests customers used to put off are suddenly easy to make, so they'll make more of them. That's good news for policyholders, but for the teams on the receiving end, it's a lot more work arriving through the same inbox.” —* ***Aman Gour*** *, Co-Founder and CEO of FurtherAI*


## **What happened when we asked for our own COI**


Our landlord needed a COI with them added to our policy. It is about as routine as commercial insurance requests get, and almost every business that leases space runs into it sooner or later.


The asking part was fast. We used AI to put together a clear request with everything the other side would need, and it was ready to send almost instantly.


But then it landed in an inbox, and from there it moved at the speed of the process behind it. We can't see exactly how many hands it passed through, but we do know how long it took: 27 days from request to certificate.


The thing is that nobody on the other end did anything wrong. They were working inside a system built for a world where requests trickled in one at a time, written by people who had already decided the request was worth the hassle.


## **Now picture that mismatch across millions of customers**


Now imagine every commercial policyholder with an agent that sends requests in seconds and follows up until it gets an answer. Volume climbs, follow-ups climb with it, and because asking takes 10 seconds, waiting a week feels like something is broken.


Meanwhile, the people doing the work haven't multiplied. They have the same hours in the day and the same patchwork of systems they've always had, with the policy admin system in one place, the inbox in another, and approvals living somewhere else again.


> *“Making a request now takes seconds, but fulfilling it can still take days. That gap is where the pressure builds, and I believe it'll keep building until service quality breaks down or the infrastructure behind it changes.” —* ***Aman Gour*** *, Co-Founder and CEO of FurtherAI*


## **Insurance needs AI that finishes the job**


Most AI in insurance so far has focused on the front of the process, which largely makes it easier to ask. Delivering is the harder half of the job. For a request like ours, that means AI that finds the policy, checks the change, prepares the certificate, and sends it back, bringing in a person only when a decision needs judgment.


That’s what we build at FurtherAI: AI agents that fulfill requests from start to finish, with people in control of the calls that need them.
